Subspace-Decomposed JEPAs: Disentangling Progression and Content in Latent World Models

Lucas Thil Affiliation: LIX, École Polytechnique Affiliation: IRT SystemX Affiliation: Palaiseau, France Email: lix@polytechnique.fr    Jesse Read Affiliation: LIX, École Polytechnique Affiliation: Palaiseau, France    Rim Kaddah Affiliation: IRT SystemX Affiliation: Palaiseau, France    Guillaume Doquet Affiliation: Safran Tech Affiliation: Chateaufort, France
Abstract

Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) learn compact latent world models by predicting future embeddings, but no single coordinate of the latent is designated to encode task progression. We carve the JEPA latent into two orthogonal subspaces with disjoint roles: a low-dimensional progression subspace 𝒛prog∈ℝk\bm{z}^{\text{prog}}\in\mathbb{R}^{k} shaped by a cosine-margin triplet loss, and a high-dimensional content subspace 𝒛cont∈ℝD−k\bm{z}^{\text{cont}}\in\mathbb{R}^{D-k} regularised by the existing SIGReg objective of LeWM. We prove that the two anti-collapse forces act on disjoint coordinates, so they compose additively rather than competing on the same dimensions. Our method, SD-JEPA improves over the LeWM baseline on the majority of its control benchmarks at matched compute, and outperforms the strongest non-LeWM JEPA baseline on Push-T; a subspace-ablation falsifier confirms the split is the load-bearing ingredient. Beyond planning, the resulting 1-D angular progression coordinate θt=atan2⁡(𝒛2prog,𝒛1prog)\theta_{t}=\mathrm{atan2}(\bm{z}^{\text{prog}}_{2},\bm{z}^{\text{prog}}_{1}) functions as a scene-aware compass on the latent. It advances with task progress, regresses when the agent backtracks, and under controlled perturbations both spikes and relocalises to a semantically appropriate new task-phase sector, separating the moment of surprise from its meaning in a way that prediction-error scalars cannot. Three quantitative tests back this up: |Δ​θt||\Delta\theta_{t}| outperforms the standard latent-prediction-error surprise (z-MSE) at localising semantic events on 4040 held-out cube episodes by up to +0.18+0.18 pooled AUROC (97.5%97.5\% per-episode win rate at ±1\pm 1-step tolerance); a within-episode linear probe across all four environments (4040 episodes per env) shows the 88-dimensional progression subspace (4.2%4.2\% of the latent) explains 7272–95%95\% of task-progress variance, with the largest probe-vs-clock gap on Reacher tracking the only env with a robust 𝒛prog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}}-aware planning lift. Code at https://github.com/LucasStill/SD-JEPA

1 Introduction

World models aim at predicting the consequences of actions in a compact latent space so that agents can plan, imagine, and generalize. Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) (LeCun and others, 2022; Assran et al., 2023; Bardes et al., 2024; Assran et al., 2025) pursue this in feature space, forgoing pixel-level reconstruction. The recent LeWM method (Maes et al., 2026) establishes an end-to-end pixel JEPA with a two-term loss, next-embedding MSE plus a Sketch Isotropic Gaussian Regularizer (SIGReg) Balestriero and LeCun (2025) on the marginal latent distribution, and demonstrates competitive planning with ∼\sim15M parameters trainable on a single GPU.

A recurring observation across LeWM and adjacent work is that these latents capture slow features and exhibit emergent temporal straightening (Hénaff et al., 2019; Sobal et al., 2022), but they do not carry an interpretable notion of progression: there is no axis along the latent whose value corresponds to “how far along” the agent is in an episode, nor any geometric prior that different episodes of the same task should share a common progression manifold.

A natural way to add a designated progression axis is to allocate a low-dimensional subspace of the latent to it, and shape that subspace with a temporal-ordering objective. Cosine-margin triplet losses are a well-established mechanism for this purpose in temporal contrastive learning (Dwibedi et al., 2019; Schneider et al., 2023): they pull embeddings of temporally adjacent frames together and push apart frames that are far in time, thereby imposing a smooth ordering on the resulting representation. Independently, recent work on temporal straightening for latent planning (Wang et al., 2026) demonstrates that geometric regularisers on latent trajectories can substantially improve gradient-based planners. What has not been studied is whether such structured-progression objectives can be combined with the marginal-distribution anti-collapse mechanisms used by end-to-end JEPAs (specifically, SIGReg in LeWM) without the two regularisers interfering.

This paper asks: can we add a structured progression coordinate to a LeWM-style JEPA latent without breaking its SIGReg anti-collapse guarantee, and does the resulting architecture improve planning?

Contributions.

  1. 1.

    We introduce SD-JEPA, an extension of LeWM that splits the JEPA latent into a low-dimensional progression subspace 𝒛prog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}} and a high-dimensional content subspace 𝒛cont\bm{z}^{\mathrm{cont}}, shaped respectively by a cosine-margin triplet loss and SIGReg.

  2. 2.

    We prove that the two anti-collapse forces (SIGReg on 𝒛cont\bm{z}^{\mathrm{cont}}, triplet on 𝒛prog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}}) act on disjoint coordinates with disjoint gradient supports, so they compose additively rather than competing on the same dimensions; we connect the triplet loss and SIGReg via the sample/dimension-contrastive duality of Garrido et al. (2023), and validate the decomposition empirically with a subspace-ablation falsifier.

  3. 3.

    We propose a planning cost that decomposes into a content term (𝒛cont\bm{z}^{\mathrm{cont}}-MSE) and an optional angular term on 𝒛prog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}}, and show that SD-JEPA matches or improves on LeWM on the majority of its control benchmarks at matched compute.

  4. 4.

    We characterise the resulting 1-D angular progression coordinate θt=atan2⁡(𝒛2prog,𝒛1prog)\theta_{t}=\mathrm{atan2}(\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}}_{2},\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}}_{1}) as a scene-aware compass on the latent: it tracks task progress, regresses under genuine task regression, and under controlled perturbations decouples the moment of surprise from its post-perturbation re-localisation.

2 Background

2.1 Notation and setting

We follow the LeWM setting. An offline dataset of trajectories {(o1:Tu,a1:Tu)}u=1U\{(o_{1:T_{u}},a_{1:T_{u}})\}_{u=1}^{U} is given, with pixel observations oto_{t} and action labels ata_{t}. An encoder fθf_{\theta} maps observations to latents 𝒛t=fθ​(ot)∈ℝD\bm{z}_{t}=f_{\theta}(o_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{D}, and a predictor pϕp_{\phi} models dynamics autoregressively in latent space: 𝒛^t+1=pϕ(𝒛t−H+1:t,at)\hat{\bm{z}}_{t+1}=p_{\phi}(\bm{z}_{t-H+1:t},a_{t}), where HH is the history length. Planning is performed by CEM over action sequences to minimize a latent-space cost to a goal embedding 𝒛g=fθ​(og)\bm{z}_{g}=f_{\theta}(o_{g}).

2.2 LeWM: next-embedding prediction with SIGReg

LeWM trains the encoder and predictor jointly with

ℒLeWM=‖𝒛^t+1−𝒛t+1‖22⏟ℒpred+λ​SIGReg​(𝒛),\mathcal{L}_{\text{LeWM}}=\underbrace{\|\hat{\bm{z}}_{t+1}-\bm{z}_{t+1}\|_{2}^{2}}_{\mathcal{L}_{\text{pred}}}\;+\;\lambda\,\mathrm{SIGReg}(\bm{z}), (1)

where SIGReg\mathrm{SIGReg} enforces that the marginal distribution of 𝒛\bm{z} is isotropic Gaussian. Using the Cramér–Wold theorem, SIGReg aggregates the univariate Epps–Pulley normality statistic over MM random unit directions u(m)∈𝕊D−1u^{(m)}\in\mathbb{S}^{D-1}:

SIGReg⁡(Z)=1M​∑m=1MT⁡(Z​u(m)),\mathrm{SIGReg}(Z)=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}T\!\left(Zu^{(m)}\right), (2)

with T⁡(⋅)T(\cdot) the Epps–Pulley test statistic. The key property of (2) is that it constrains only the marginal distribution p⁡(𝒛)p(\bm{z}); the conditional p⁡(𝒛t+1∣𝒛t)p(\bm{z}_{t+1}\mid\bm{z}_{t}) is unaffected.

2.3 Duality of contrastive and covariance-based regularizers

Garrido et al. (2023) show that the sample-contrastive criterion ℒc=‖K⊤​K−diag⁡(K⊤​K)‖F2\mathcal{L}_{c}=\|K^{\top}K-\mathrm{diag}(K^{\top}K)\|_{F}^{2} and the dimension-contrastive criterion ℒn​c=‖K​K⊤−diag⁡(K​K⊤)‖F2\mathcal{L}_{nc}=\|KK^{\top}-\mathrm{diag}(KK^{\top})\|_{F}^{2} (with KK the embedding matrix) are equivalent up to the row- and column-norms of KK:

ℒn​c+∑j=1M‖Kj,⋅‖24=ℒc+∑i=1N‖K⋅,i‖24.\mathcal{L}_{nc}+\sum_{j=1}^{M}\|K_{j,\cdot}\|_{2}^{4}=\mathcal{L}_{c}+\sum_{i=1}^{N}\|K_{\cdot,i}\|_{2}^{4}. (3)

Under double-L2L_{2}-normalization of rows and columns, ℒn​c=ℒc+N−M\mathcal{L}_{nc}=\mathcal{L}_{c}+N-M. SIGReg and the cosine-triplet both belong to this broader variance-repulsion family, a fact we exploit in §4.

3 Method: SD-JEPA

3.1 Subspace decomposition of the latent

We split the JEPA latent into a progression subspace and a content subspace:

𝒛t=P​𝒛tprog⏟∈ℝD+Q​𝒛tcont⏟∈ℝD,𝒛tprog∈ℝk,𝒛tcont∈ℝD−k,\bm{z}_{t}=\underbrace{P\,\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}}_{t}}_{\in\mathbb{R}^{D}}\;+\;\underbrace{Q\,\bm{z}^{\mathrm{cont}}_{t}}_{\in\mathbb{R}^{D}},\qquad\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{k},\ \bm{z}^{\mathrm{cont}}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{D-k}, (4)

where P∈ℝD×kP\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times k} and Q∈ℝD×(D−k)Q\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times(D-k)} are fixed orthogonal injections with P⊤​P=IkP^{\top}P=I_{k}, Q⊤​Q=ID−kQ^{\top}Q=I_{D-k}, P⊤​Q=0P^{\top}Q=0. In practice we take the canonical split P=[Ik; 0]P=[I_{k};\,0], Q=[0;ID−k]Q=[0;\,I_{D-k}], so that 𝒛tprog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}}_{t} and 𝒛tcont\bm{z}^{\mathrm{cont}}_{t} are simply the first kk and last D−kD-k coordinates of 𝒛t\bm{z}_{t}. We use k=2k=2 by default.

3.2 Four-term training objective

SD-JEPA is trained with

ℒSD=ℒpred​(𝒛)+λS​SIGReg​(𝒛cont)+λT​ℒtrip​(𝒛prog)+λstr​ℒstraight​(𝒛)\mathcal{L}_{\text{SD}}\;=\;\mathcal{L}_{\text{pred}}(\bm{z})\;+\;\lambda_{S}\,\mathrm{SIGReg}(\bm{z}^{\mathrm{cont}})\;+\;\lambda_{T}\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{trip}}(\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}})\;+\;\lambda_{\mathrm{str}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{straight}}(\bm{z}) (5)

with:

  • •

    ℒpred​(𝒛)=‖𝒛^t+1−𝒛t+1‖22\mathcal{L}_{\text{pred}}(\bm{z})=\|\hat{\bm{z}}_{t+1}-\bm{z}_{t+1}\|_{2}^{2} on the full latent (unchanged from LeWM).

  • •

    SIGReg⁡(𝒛cont)\mathrm{SIGReg}(\bm{z}^{\mathrm{cont}}): SIGReg ((2)) applied only to the content subspace, using random unit directions sampled in ℝD−k\mathbb{R}^{D-k}.

  • •

    ℒtrip​(𝒛prog)\mathcal{L}_{\text{trip}}(\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}}): a cosine-margin triplet loss on 𝒛prog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}} that orders embeddings by their position within a trajectory: positives are sampled within a temporal window ϑt\vartheta_{t} of an anchor, negatives outside the window or from a different trajectory.

  • •

    ℒstraight​(𝒛)=−𝔼t​[cos⁡(𝒗t,𝒗t+1)]\mathcal{L}_{\text{straight}}(\bm{z})=-\mathbb{E}_{t}\!\left[\cos(\bm{v}_{t},\bm{v}_{t+1})\right] with 𝒗t=𝒛t+1−𝒛t\bm{v}_{t}=\bm{z}_{t+1}-\bm{z}_{t}: explicit temporal straightening (see §A.3).

The LeWM base is recovered as λT=λP=λstr=0\lambda_{T}=\lambda_{P}=\lambda_{\mathrm{str}}=0 and applying SIGReg\mathrm{SIGReg} to the full 𝒛\bm{z} instead of 𝒛cont\bm{z}^{\mathrm{cont}}.

3.3 Latent-space indicators as predictor conditioning

From 𝒛tprog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}}_{t} we compute the angular and radial readouts

θt=atan2⁡(𝒛t,2prog,𝒛t,1prog),rt=‖𝒛tprog‖2.\theta_{t}=\mathrm{atan2}(\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}}_{t,2},\,\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}}_{t,1}),\qquad r_{t}=\|\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}}_{t}\|_{2}. (6)

These are scalar, scale- and rotation-aware quantities that summarize where on the progression manifold the current state sits. We expose them to the autoregressive predictor as additional conditioning alongside the action embedding:

𝒛^t+1=pϕ(𝒛t−H+1:t,at,(θt,rt)).\hat{\bm{z}}_{t+1}=p_{\phi}\!\left(\bm{z}_{t-H+1:t},\;a_{t},\;(\theta_{t},r_{t})\right). (7)

Concretely, (θt,rt)(\theta_{t},r_{t}) (with θt\theta_{t} encoded as (sin⁡θt,cos⁡θt)(\sin\theta_{t},\cos\theta_{t}) to avoid wrap-around discontinuities) is embedded to the predictor’s hidden dimension and summed with the action embedding before AdaLN-zero conditioning. This gives the predictor an explicit progression compass, analogous in spirit to sinusoidal positional encodings in attention: no new information, but better-structured information.

3.4 Planning with an angular goal-matching cost

In LeWM, planning minimizes ‖𝒛^H−𝒛g‖22\|\hat{\bm{z}}_{H}-\bm{z}_{g}\|_{2}^{2} at the end of a rollout. We replace this with a decomposed cost:

C⁡(𝒛^H)=‖𝒛cont^H−𝒛gcont‖22⏟content match+γ​(1−cos⁡(θ^H,θg))⏟angular progression match+δ​(r^H−rg)2⏟radial match.C(\hat{\bm{z}}_{H})=\underbrace{\|\hat{\bm{z}^{\mathrm{cont}}}_{H}-\bm{z}^{\mathrm{cont}}_{g}\|_{2}^{2}}_{\text{content match}}\;+\;\gamma\,\underbrace{\bigl(1-\cos(\hat{\theta}_{H},\theta_{g})\bigr)}_{\text{angular progression match}}\;+\;\delta\,\underbrace{(\hat{r}_{H}-r_{g})^{2}}_{\text{radial match}}. (8)

The angular and radial terms make the progression match scale-invariant and independent of the ambient content geometry. The receding-horizon Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) solver is otherwise identical to LeWM: at each replanning step, 300300 candidate action sequences are sampled, the top-3030 retained as elites to update the sampling Gaussian, and we iterate 3030 times on Push-T and 1010 times on the other environments.

4 Theoretical analysis

We state the two propositions that establish why the subspace split composes additively rather than competing on the same dimensions. Full proofs and three further results (consistency with emergent straightening, identifiability of the progression axis, when the split fails) are deferred to App. A.

Proposition 1 (Disjoint gradient supports).

Let 𝐳∈ℝD\bm{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} be written as 𝐳=P​𝐳prog+Q​𝐳cont\bm{z}=P\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}}+Q\bm{z}^{\mathrm{cont}} with P⊤​P=IkP^{\top}P=I_{k}, Q⊤​Q=ID−kQ^{\top}Q=I_{D-k}, P⊤​Q=0P^{\top}Q=0 (§3). Let SIGReg\mathrm{SIGReg} be applied on 𝐳cont\bm{z}^{\mathrm{cont}} and any function ℒ\mathcal{L} on 𝐳prog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}} alone. Then span⁡(∇𝐳SIGReg​(Q⊤​𝐳))⊆col⁡(Q)\mathrm{span}(\nabla_{\bm{z}}\,\mathrm{SIGReg}(Q^{\top}\bm{z}))\subseteq\mathrm{col}(Q), span⁡(∇𝐳ℒ​(P⊤​𝐳))⊆col⁡(P)\mathrm{span}(\nabla_{\bm{z}}\,\mathcal{L}(P^{\top}\bm{z}))\subseteq\mathrm{col}(P), and these two subspaces are orthogonal.

Proof sketch. SIGReg⁡(Q⊤​𝒛)\mathrm{SIGReg}(Q^{\top}\bm{z}) depends on 𝒛\bm{z} only through Q⊤​𝒛Q^{\top}\bm{z}, so by the chain rule ∇𝒛SIGReg​(Q⊤​𝒛)=Q​∇𝒛contSIGReg​(𝒛cont)\nabla_{\bm{z}}\,\mathrm{SIGReg}(Q^{\top}\bm{z})=Q\,\nabla_{\bm{z}^{\mathrm{cont}}}\mathrm{SIGReg}(\bm{z}^{\mathrm{cont}}), which lies in col⁡(Q)\mathrm{col}(Q). Identically for ℒ\mathcal{L} and PP. Orthogonality follows from P⊤​Q=0P^{\top}Q=0. □\square

Proposition 2 (No double-counting on orthogonal subspaces).

Let ℒtrip\mathcal{L}_{\text{trip}} act on 𝐳prog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}} and SIGReg\mathrm{SIGReg} act on 𝐳cont\bm{z}^{\mathrm{cont}}. Under the split, their anti-collapse gradients act on orthogonal coordinates: removing either term cannot be compensated by increasing the other (the other has no gradient in the affected directions).

These two results together formalise the architectural intuition: triplet on 𝒛prog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}} and SIGReg on 𝒛cont\bm{z}^{\mathrm{cont}} are complementary rather than redundant despite belonging to the same variance-repulsion family in the sense of Garrido et al. (2023). The empirical falsifier (A2_full == A0, Tab. 2) confirms the proposition matters in practice: when the split is removed and triplet acts on the full latent, the gain disappears. Disjointness is at the latent level; the encoder’s parameter gradients are still the sum of both terms via the chain rule, so encoder-level conflict is not formally precluded.

5 Experiments

5.1 Setup

We evaluate SD-JEPA on the four control benchmarks of Maes et al. (2026): Two-Room (2-D navigation), Reacher (DM-Control), Push-T (2-D manipulation), and OGBench-Cube (3-D manipulation). All evaluations use the paper’s protocol, 5050-step horizon, 2525-step goal offset, CEM solver with 300300 candidates / 3030 iterations on Push-T and 1010 iterations elsewhere, planning horizon 55 at frame-skip 55. We train each model for 10 epochs at batch size 128128, matching the LeWM training budget; encoder and predictor architectures are inherited from LeWM (ViT-tiny encoder, 66-layer transformer predictor, ∼18{\sim}18M parameters total). Multi-seed runs use seeds {0,42,3072}\{0,42,3072\}. Implementation details, dataset paths, hyperparameters, and a glossary of the ablation rung names (A0, A2, A2_full, A4, A5, A6) used throughout this section are in App. C and Tab. 6.

5.2 Main results

Figure 1 shows planning success rate per environment for SD-JEPA against the published LeWM numbers and the cross-method baselines reported by Maes et al. (2026). SD-JEPA improves over LeWM on three of the four environments at matched 10-epoch compute:

  • •

    Reacher: +2+2 over LeWM (86→8886\to 88 at kprog=4k_{\text{prog}}{=}4, 33-seed mean across both planning costs); +12+12 over our A0 rerun (7676).

  • •

    Two-Room: +3+3 over LeWM (87→9087\to 90 at kprog=2k_{\text{prog}}{=}2, 33-seed mean).

  • •

    Push-T: +1.3+1.3 over LeWM (96→97.396\to 97.3 at kprog=8k_{\text{prog}}{=}8, 33-seed mean),+5+5 over the strongest non-LeWM baseline (DINO-WM with proprioception, 9292).

  • •

    OGBench-Cube: −2-2 vs LeWM at kprog=2k_{\text{prog}}{=}2 (7272 vs 7474, 33-seed mean); the kprog={4,8}k_{\text{prog}}{=}\{4,8\} sweep does not close the gap (cube prefers k=2k{=}2 in our 10-epoch regime).

The optimal kprogk_{\text{prog}} is task-dependent (§5.4); the architectural framework is robust across k∈{2,4,8}k\in\{2,4,8\}. Table 1 reports cross-method numbers.

5.3 The subspace split is load-bearing

To isolate which component of SD-JEPA drives the gain, two falsifiers on Push-T (Tab. 2, single seed). A2_full disables the split: 96=96= A0. A2_split_full keeps the split but mis-targets the triplet on the full latent: 9292, four points below A0. The split itself, not the triplet in isolation, is the load-bearing ingredient: the empirical analogue of Prop. 2 on the actual training dynamics.

5.4 kprogk_{\text{prog}} scales with task complexity

The optimal kprogk_{\text{prog}} varies per env (Tab. 3). On Push-T, multi-seed evaluation gives a clean monotone 94→96→97.394\to 96\to 97.3 at k∈{2,4,8}k\in\{2,4,8\}, with the k=8k{=}8 checkpoint exhibiting a near-perfect S1S^{1} progression manifold (σr∈[0.04,0.07]\sigma_{r}\in[0.04,0.07], angular span 6.16.1 rad on seven held-out episodes; App. E). Two-Room is non-monotone (k=2k{=}2 and k=8k{=}8 both 9090, k=4k{=}4 at 8888), consistent with the 1-D navigation topology saturating at two progression dimensions; Reacher prefers a moderate k=4k{=}4 (9292 vs. 8484/8282). The cross-env pattern is not “higher kk always wins” but “the right kk matches the task’s intrinsic progression dimensionality.” A negative control with 𝒛prog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}}-only MSE planning collapses to 28%28\% on Push-T: the progression subspace is too low-dimensional to carry goal information alone; the gain at higher kk comes from the encoder devoting more budget to a coherent progression manifold while the planning cost still operates primarily on 𝒛cont\bm{z}^{\mathrm{cont}}.

5.5 The latent acts as a scene-aware compass

The canonical SD-JEPA architecture exposes a 1-D angular readout θt=atan2⁡(𝒛t,2prog,𝒛t,1prog)\theta_{t}=\mathrm{atan2}(\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}}_{t,2},\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}}_{t,1}) on the trained progression subspace. We probe what this coordinate captures along three axes: the cross-episode geometry it produces in 𝒛prog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}} versus 𝒛cont\bm{z}^{\mathrm{cont}}, the physical task quantities it correlates with across environments, and how it behaves under controlled observation perturbations. The picture is environment-dependent and partly clock-like, partly task-coupled; the full per-environment breakdown is in App. E.

Cross-episode geometry matches the disjoint-supports prediction.

Prop. 1 predicts that 𝒛prog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}} should carry shared cross-episode progression structure while 𝒛cont\bm{z}^{\mathrm{cont}} should be episode-specific. The Push-T A2 t-SNE (Fig. 4, App. E) makes the asymmetry visible: 𝒛cont\bm{z}^{\mathrm{cont}} separates into per-episode clusters while 𝒛prog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}}’s arcs partially mix across episodes. The second moments confirm it: cos¯​(𝒛prog​[t])≈0.5\overline{\cos}(\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}}[t])\approx 0.5 vs. cos¯​(𝒛cont​[t])≈0\overline{\cos}(\bm{z}^{\mathrm{cont}}[t])\approx 0, with the full 𝒛\bm{z} inheriting the 𝒛cont\bm{z}^{\mathrm{cont}}-side near-orthogonality.

θt\theta_{t} is partly a clock and partly a task-phase coordinate, with the balance varying by env and kprogk_{\mathrm{prog}}.

We score the per-episode Spearman ρ\rho between θt\theta_{t} and candidate proxies: the elapsed-time clock (step_idx) plus env-specific physical quantities (block_target_dist on Cube, ee_target_dist on Reacher, block_angle_err on Push-T). Mean |ρ||\rho| tables, heatmaps, and per-episode signed values are in App. E. Cube is the only env where a task-physical signal beats the clock (block_target_dist, |ρ|=0.59|\rho|{=}0.59 vs 0.470.47); elsewhere the two are within 0.10.1 or the clock leads. On Push-T, |ρ||\rho| with the clock falls from 0.910.91 at k=2k{=}2 to 0.560.56 at k=8k{=}8 as the physical signals catch up, consistent with θ\theta becoming more cyclic-phase-like at higher kk. The cube state-traj overlay (Fig. 4, App. E) makes one episode concrete: θ\theta traces a smooth phase gradient along the planar trajectory.

θt\theta_{t} as a richer surprise signal: separating the moment of surprise from its meaning.

Standard latent VoE, ‖𝒛^t+1−𝒛t+1‖\|\hat{\bm{z}}_{t+1}-\bm{z}_{t+1}\|, says when the model was wrong but not about what; identical scalar magnitudes may correspond to different counterfactual interpretations. We test the angular signal on Push-T with a teleport-and-continue perturbation: at step 5050 of held-out episode 00, the next observation is replaced by a frame from episode 10001000 (whose T-block sits on the opposite side of the goal) and the planner resumes. Two distinct signals appear in θt\theta_{t} (Fig. 3). (i) A sharp single-frame spike of ∼1.5{\sim}1.5 rad in |Δ​θt||\Delta\theta_{t}| (≈75×\approx 75\times baseline drift) marks the moment, like a scalar VoE spike. (ii) After the spike, θt\theta_{t} does not return: it relocalises from sector θ≈−2.5\theta\!\approx\!-2.5 to sector θ≈−4.0\theta\!\approx\!-4.0, corresponding to the new solving mode (T-block on the other side), marking the meaning, the model’s updated belief about which task phase is active. Standard MSE-VoE reports only the spike, not the re-localisation. Three further perturbation modes (splice, 1-frame teleport, reverse) reproduce this pattern (App. F).

|Δ​θt||\Delta\theta_{t}| outperforms scalar prediction-error at localising semantic phase events.

The qualitative argument above motivates a quantitative test: does |Δ​θt||\Delta\theta_{t}| actually pinpoint task-meaningful events more reliably than the latent prediction-error magnitude ‖𝒛^t+1−𝒛t+1‖\|\hat{\bm{z}}_{t+1}-\bm{z}_{t+1}\| (z-MSE), the standard surprise metric in latent world models? On OGBench-Cube the gripper-contact transitions provide an objective ground-truth event signal: each pick-and-place episode has roughly four such transitions (close, open, close, open) marking semantically meaningful phase boundaries. We compute the per-step AUROC of each surprise metric against labels marking “step is within ±tol\pm\mathrm{tol} of any contact transition” on 4040 held-out episodes (160160 ground-truth events, 14801480 steps; SD-JEPA kprog=8k_{\mathrm{prog}}{=}8 checkpoint). Pooled AUROC and the per-episode head-to-head appear in Tab. 4; the qualitative phase overlay on episode 500500 is shown in Fig. 2 and the four-panel summary across all episodes in Fig. 14 (App. G).

𝒛prog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}} packs within-episode progress information densely.

A complementary test asks how much task-progress information is packed into the progression subspace per dimension. We fit linear-regression probes from various latent features to a per-episode-normalised target-distance signal, in two regimes: a per-episode probe (within each held-out episode, leave-one-step-out CV; mean R2 over 4040 episodes) and a pooled probe (leave 25%25\% of episodes out, 3030 bootstraps). On cube, the per-episode probe gives 𝒛prog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}} (88 dims, 4.2%4.2\% of the latent) mean R2=0.905{}^{2}=\mathbf{0.905} (𝟏𝟎𝟎%\mathbf{100\%} positive over 4040 episodes); (sin⁡θ,cos⁡θ)(\sin\theta,\cos\theta) packs 55.5%\mathbf{55.5\%} of the variance into just 22 dimensions, 2×2\times a random-22-d projection of 𝒛\bm{z} (0.2630.263) and the elapsed-time clock (0.2910.291). Cross-env replication on the same 4040-episode-per-env protocol confirms the claim is not cube-specific (Tab. 5): 𝒛prog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}} R∈2{0.91,0.91,0.95,0.72}{}^{2}\in\{0.91,0.91,0.95,0.72\} on cube/Push-T/Reacher/Two-Room, 100%100\% positive on the first three and 95%95\% on Two-Room, never below 0.720.72 across any env using only 4.2%4.2\% of the latent. The largest probe-vs-clock gap, +0.66+0.66 on Reacher, lines up with Reacher being the only env with a robust 𝒛prog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}}-aware planning lift (§5.6, App. D). The pooled probe is the honest caveat: across episodes with different absolute initial distances, only step_idx stays reliably positive (App. G, Tab. 9, Fig. 16, 17); the compass is a per-trajectory phase coordinate, not a globally calibrated cross-episode distance estimate.

Three operationalisations of the same intuition.

The phase-event AUROC (Tab. 4, |Δ​θt||\Delta\theta_{t}| wins on 39/4039/40 cube episodes) asks where the semantic events are; the regime-change CPD (App. G) asks where the regime boundaries are; the linear probe (Tab. 9, App. G) asks how much progress information is packed per dimension. All three confirm that the trained 𝒛prog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}} subspace, and θ\theta in particular, carries task-phase structure that the standard scalar prediction-error metric does not surface.

5.6 Cross-environment summary and limitations

SD-JEPA improves on three of four LeWM envs (Tab. 1, Tab. 3, 33-seed multi-seed); the framework is robust across kprog∈{2,4,8}k_{\text{prog}}\in\{2,4,8\} but the per-env optimum varies. Whether full-z planning helps is also task-dependent (Reacher +3.3+3.3 pp at k=8k{=}8, other envs within ±1\pm 1 pp; App. D). The latent-geometry diagnostics establish that the architecture produces the predicted progression-content geometry independently of any planning-success delta, providing a second axis of evidence on top of the empirical one.

Known limitations.

(i) Per-environment kprogk_{\text{prog}} tuning means we report best-kk values rather than a single universal kk. (ii) The triplet and angular readouts both use cosine geometry; other distance metrics or non-angular readouts (e.g. a learned scalar progression head) may surface complementary structure. (iii) The fixed orthogonal [P,Q][P,Q] is a modeling choice; a learned orthogonal decomposition is the natural extension. Extended ablations on auxiliary terms (straightening, polar conditioning, angular planning cost) are in App. D.

6 Related work

Latent world models.

We complete the related work mentioned in the introduction with pixel-space architectures such as DreamerV3 Hafner et al. (2024) and feature-space JEPAs include I-JEPA, V-JEPA, PLDM, DINO-WM, and most directly LeWM (LeCun and others, 2022; Assran et al., 2023; Bardes et al., 2024; Sobal et al., 2022; Maes et al., 2026). Latent-action world models such as LAWM, Genie, Gaia-2, Cosmos and explore alternative conditioning regimes (Garrido et al., 2026; Bruce et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2024; Team et al., 2025; Russell et al., 2025; Agarwal et al., 2025). SD-JEPA inherits LeWM’s encoder-predictor stack and the SIGReg anti-collapse regularizer, adding only a fixed orthogonal subspace split and a triplet term on the progression side; the parameter count is identical to LeWM (18.0418.04M, no new learnable weights).

Progression geometry and temporal straightening.

The cosine-margin triplet on 𝒛prog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}} is a temporal-ordering loss in the family of Dwibedi et al. (2019); Schneider et al. (2023). Our straightening regulariser ℒstraight=−𝔼⁡[cos⁡(𝒗t,𝒗t+1)]\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{straight}}=-\mathbb{E}[\cos(\bm{v}_{t},\bm{v}_{t+1})] is identical to the curvature loss of Wang et al. (2026) (stop-gradient anti-collapse, gradient-descent planner). On Push-T at the matched protocol, their best published configuration reaches 91.3±2.591.3\pm 2.5; SD-JEPA at kprog=8k_{\text{prog}}{=}8 reaches 97.3±1.297.3\pm 1.2, 66 points above. Adding the curvature regulariser on top of SIGReg in our setup (rung A4, App. D) costs 1414 points on Push-T, consistent with the principle that anti-collapse forces should not compete on the same coordinates. Latent straightening has applications in OOD detection Internò et al. (2025). The SSL duality framework of Garrido et al. (2023) grounds our no-double-counting result.

7 Discussion

The latent as a navigable map.

The diagnostics in §5.5 support reading θt\theta_{t} as less of a chronological counter and more of a state-based navigation signal: it advances with task progress, regresses in lockstep when the agent backtracks, and under perturbation jumps to a semantically appropriate new sector. The qualitative parallel with mammalian head-direction cells (Taube et al., 1990; Knierim and Hamilton, 2011) is suggestive; we make no mechanistic claim. App. F reproduces the moment-and-meaning decoupling under three further perturbation modes.

When does θ\theta-coupling translate into a planning lift?

The full-z planning lift is non-uniform: Reacher gains +3.3+3.3 pp at kprog=8k_{\mathrm{prog}}{=}8, Cube +2.0+2.0, Two-Room and Push-T nothing. Cross-referencing per-environment θ\theta-task coupling (App. E), θ\theta-coupling is necessary but not sufficient: Reacher (coupling |ρ|=0.49|\rho|=0.49) sees the cleanest lift; Two-Room (0.340.34) sees none. The two anomalies have separate bottlenecks: Cube has the strongest coupling (0.590.59) but the predictor’s contact-rich rollout error caps the cost-function gain, while Push-T at kprog=8k_{\mathrm{prog}}{=}8 is already near the ceiling (97.3%97.3\%). Reacher sits in the sweet spot: phase-coupled enough for the angular cost to add information, simple-enough dynamics that the predictor is not the bottleneck. The cross-environment probe (Tab. 5) gives a complementary mechanistic story for the same pattern: Reacher has the largest within-episode probe-vs-clock gap (+0.66+0.66 R2, the largest in our suite), so the encoder concentrates the most progress information into 𝒛prog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}} exactly where the planning cost can exploit it.

What θt\theta_{t} adds beyond scalar VoE.

The angular readout differs from ‖𝒛^t+1−𝒛t+1‖\|\hat{\bm{z}}_{t+1}-\bm{z}_{t+1}\| in three ways: it reports a phase sector, it is signed, and it is cross-environment comparable on a unit circle. The three tests of §5.5 confirm complementarity rather than competition with VoE; the broader design space of geometric readouts of structured-latent world models is an open agenda.

8 Conclusion

SD-JEPA splits the JEPA latent into a low-dimensional progression subspace shaped by a cosine-margin triplet loss and a high-dimensional content subspace regularised by SIGReg. We prove the two anti-collapse forces act on disjoint coordinates and validate this empirically: removing the split collapses the architectural gain back to the LeWM baseline. At matched 10-epoch compute (3-seed multi-seed) SD-JEPA improves on three of four LeWM control benchmarks (Two-Room +3+3, Reacher +2+2, Push-T +1.3+1.3; cube −2-2). Beyond planning, the 1-D angular coordinate θt\theta_{t} behaves as a scene-aware compass that tracks progress, regresses on backtrack, and under perturbations separates the moment of surprise from its meaning. Three independent quantitative tests back this up: |Δ​θt||\Delta\theta_{t}| beats z-MSE at semantic-event localisation on 4040 cube episodes (+0.18+0.18 pooled AUROC at ±1\pm 1-step tolerance, 39/4039/40 per-episode wins), change-point detection on the angular-velocity trace beats prediction-error metrics at loose tolerance, and a within-episode linear probe replicates across all four envs (4040 episodes per env) with 𝒛prog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}} R∈2[0.72,0.95]{}^{2}\in[0.72,0.95] using only 4.2%4.2\% of the latent. All three back the same conclusion: the angular readout extends the standard interpretability toolkit with information the scalar prediction-error metric does not supply.

Appendix A Extended theoretical analysis

This appendix reproduces the full theoretical content compressed into §4, including the corollary on the marginal product structure, the Garrido-style duality discussion, and three further results (consistency with emergent straightening, identifiability of the progression axis, and conditions under which the split fails).

A.1 Non-conflict under the subspace split

Proposition 3 (Disjoint gradient supports).

Let 𝐳∈ℝD\bm{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} be written as 𝐳=P​𝐳prog+Q​𝐳cont\bm{z}=P\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}}+Q\bm{z}^{\mathrm{cont}} with P,QP,Q as in §3, and let SIGReg\mathrm{SIGReg} be applied on 𝐳cont\bm{z}^{\mathrm{cont}} and ℒ\mathcal{L} on 𝐳prog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}}. Then for every sample,

span⁡(∇𝒛SIGReg​(Q⊤​𝒛))⊆col⁡(Q),span⁡(∇𝒛ℒ​(P⊤​𝒛))⊆col⁡(P),\mathrm{span}\!\left(\nabla_{\bm{z}}\,\mathrm{SIGReg}(Q^{\top}\bm{z})\right)\;\subseteq\;\mathrm{col}(Q),\qquad\mathrm{span}\!\left(\nabla_{\bm{z}}\,\mathcal{L}(P^{\top}\bm{z})\right)\;\subseteq\;\mathrm{col}(P), (9)

and these two subspaces are orthogonal.

Proof sketch.

SIGReg⁡(Q⊤​𝒛)\mathrm{SIGReg}(Q^{\top}\bm{z}) depends on 𝒛\bm{z} only through Q⊤​𝒛Q^{\top}\bm{z}, so its gradient with respect to 𝒛\bm{z} factors through QQ: ∇𝒛SIGReg​(Q⊤​𝒛)=Q​∇𝒛contSIGReg​(𝒛cont)\nabla_{\bm{z}}\,\mathrm{SIGReg}(Q^{\top}\bm{z})=Q\,\nabla_{\bm{z}^{\mathrm{cont}}}\mathrm{SIGReg}(\bm{z}^{\mathrm{cont}}). Identically for the second loss ℒ\mathcal{L} on 𝒛prog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}} and PP. Orthogonality P⊤​Q=0P^{\top}Q=0 gives the conclusion. ∎

Proposition 1 formalises the informal claim that an arbitrary loss on 𝒛prog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}} alone does not interfere with SIGReg on 𝒛cont\bm{z}^{\mathrm{cont}}. The triplet loss on 𝒛prog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}} and the prediction loss on the full 𝒛\bm{z} do have components in col⁡(Q)\mathrm{col}(Q) (through the content subspace of the predictor output), so the non-conflict is specifically between the marginal-distributional term on 𝒛cont\bm{z}^{\mathrm{cont}} and any progression-geometric term on 𝒛prog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}}.

Corollary 1.

Under the subspace split, the isotropic Gaussian constraint imposed by SIGReg\mathrm{SIGReg} holds on the marginal p⁡(𝐳cont)p(\bm{z}^{\mathrm{cont}}) regardless of the geometry imposed on p⁡(𝐳prog)p(\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}}) by any loss acting on 𝐳prog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}} alone.

A.2 Relation to the sample/dimension-contrastive duality

The cosine-margin triplet loss on 𝒛prog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}} is a sample-contrastive criterion in the sense of Garrido et al. (2023): it repels 𝒛aprog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}}_{a} from 𝒛nprog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}}_{n} while attracting it to 𝒛pprog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}}_{p}, in a space of L2L_{2}-normalized embeddings (cosine similarity is the inner product of unit vectors). SIGReg on 𝒛cont\bm{z}^{\mathrm{cont}} is not exactly a dimension-contrastive criterion, but it belongs to the same variance-repulsion family: it penalizes any departure of the marginal from isotropic Gaussian, and in particular penalizes any direction along which the variance is abnormally low (collapse) or the covariance is nonzero (feature correlation). Under the double-L2L_{2}-normalization assumption of Garrido et al. (2023), the anti-collapse force of the triplet loss on 𝒛prog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}} equals (up to additive constants) that of a VICReg-style dimension-contrastive criterion. SIGReg subsumes that variance/covariance criterion as a special case (matching the second moments of an isotropic Gaussian).

Proposition 4 (No double-counting on orthogonal subspaces).

Let ℒtrip\mathcal{L}_{\text{trip}} act on 𝐳prog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}} and SIGReg\mathrm{SIGReg} act on 𝐳cont\bm{z}^{\mathrm{cont}}. Under the subspace split, their anti-collapse gradients act on orthogonal coordinates and therefore do not duplicate: removing either term cannot be compensated by increasing the other, since the other has no gradient in the affected coordinate directions.

Proof sketch.

Apply Proposition 1 with the triplet loss as the function ℒ\mathcal{L} on 𝒛prog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}}. ∎

Proposition 2 is the practical consequence of the duality: even though triplet and SIGReg are of the same family (in the Garrido sense), on the subspace split they are complementary rather than redundant. This gives a clean theoretical justification for using both terms simultaneously rather than treating one as subsuming the other.

A.3 Consistency with emergent straightening

LeWM reports (Sec. 5 and Appendix H of (Maes et al., 2026)) that as training proceeds, the cosine similarity between consecutive latent velocity vectors 𝒗t=𝒛t+1−𝒛t\bm{v}_{t}=\bm{z}_{t+1}-\bm{z}_{t} increases emergently, without any explicit regularization. This perceptual straightening property, inspired by Hénaff et al. (2019), is an invariant of good representations of natural dynamics: straight paths in latent space are linearly extrapolable, and so compound less error over multi-step rollouts.

Our straightening term ℒstraight​(𝒛)=−𝔼⁡[cos⁡(𝒗t,𝒗t+1)]\mathcal{L}_{\text{straight}}(\bm{z})=-\mathbb{E}[\cos(\bm{v}_{t},\bm{v}_{t+1})] makes this trend explicit. It is:

  • •

    scale-invariant in 𝒛\bm{z}: cosine depends only on directions of velocity, not magnitudes; this means ℒstraight\mathcal{L}_{\text{straight}} does not compete with the variance-related component of SIGReg\mathrm{SIGReg};

  • •

    subspace-consistent: applying ℒstraight\mathcal{L}_{\text{straight}} on the full 𝒛\bm{z} does not prefer one of 𝒛prog,𝒛cont\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}},\bm{z}^{\mathrm{cont}} over the other; in practice we may apply it only on 𝒛cont\bm{z}^{\mathrm{cont}} if 𝒛prog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}} is already sufficiently constrained by the triplet ordering;

  • •

    a soft regularizer: it does not force cos=1\cos=1 (perfectly straight dynamics), only moves the population mean upward.

Proposition 5 (Soft bias towards the emergent optimum).

Let ℒLeWM\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LeWM}} denote the LeWM base loss and assume (as empirically reported) that along its optimization path 𝔼⁡[cos⁡(𝐯t,𝐯t+1)]\mathbb{E}[\cos(\bm{v}_{t},\bm{v}_{t+1})] increases monotonically toward a limit c⋆<1c^{\star}<1. Adding λstr​ℒstraight\lambda_{\mathrm{str}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{straight}} as a soft term (with λstr>0\lambda_{\mathrm{str}}>0) preserves the limiting direction of optimization: the gradient of ℒstraight\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{straight}} at the LeWM optimum is aligned with the direction of increasing straightness, hence the added term is non-antagonistic.

Empirically this is the weakest of our claims, but it rests on the reported emergence from previous works. It motivates treating straightening as a warm-start regularizer rather than a hard constraint.

A.4 Identifiability of the progression axis

Under the canonical (P,Q)(P,Q) split with k=2k=2, the angular coordinate θt=atan2⁡(𝒛2prog,𝒛1prog)\theta_{t}=\mathrm{atan2}(\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}}_{2},\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}}_{1}) is identifiable up to a global rotation (the triplet loss enforces a cyclic ordering on the unit-circle but does not pin a unique reference direction). This rotation freedom is harmless when the planning cost itself is rotation-invariant (the canonical 𝒛cont\bm{z}^{\mathrm{cont}}-MSE cost is, by construction).

The identifiability is local to episodes: episodes with different durations or solving modes can each present a coherent angular progression in 𝒛prog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}} without any global reference direction shared across them.

A.5 When does the subspace split fail?

The construction above assumes the progression subspace 𝒛prog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}} is a reasonable kk-dimensional summary of the episode phase. This assumption fails when:

  1. 1.

    The environment lacks coherent episodic temporal structure (e.g. purely exploratory rollouts with no consistent task progression). In that case the triplet loss has no useful ordering signal and the split degenerates to the LeWM baseline.

  2. 2.

    The task has multiple branching progressions (e.g. different goals per episode with no shared notion of completion). The triplet loss can still impose local orderings within each branch, but a single kk-dimensional progression manifold may not accommodate the branching cleanly; goal-conditioned variants are a natural extension.

  3. 3.

    kk is too large: the progression subspace absorbs content information, polluting the (θ,r)(\theta,r) reading. We sweep k∈{2,4,8}k\in\{2,4,8\} as an ablation.

Appendix B Implementation notes

We build on the public reference implementation of LeWM (Maes et al., 2026) for the encoder, predictor, action-conditioning, and SIGReg modules. SD-JEPA additions are localised to (a) computing the canonical injections P,QP,Q on the projected latent, (b) instantiating the cosine-margin triplet on 𝒛prog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}}, and (c) the optional polar-conditioning / angular-planning-cost paths described in App. D. The triplet uses within-batch sampling: for each anchor, a positive is drawn from the same trajectory within a temporal window ϑt\vartheta_{t} and a negative from outside that window or from a different trajectory in the same batch, so triplet computation adds negligible overhead to the standard JEPA training step.

Appendix C Hyperparameter summary

Per-environment configs, dataset paths, hyperparameter sweeps, and training-time stop conditions are documented in the released code. The base hyperparameters: AdamW, lr ×10−55\!\times\!10^{-5}, weight decay 10−310^{-3}, cosine-annealed over the 10 training epochs, batch size 128128, image resolution 224×224224\times 224, ViT-tiny encoder (patch size 1414), 66-layer transformer predictor with AdaLN-zero action conditioning, embedding dimension 192192. The frame-skip is 55 for all environments. Default loss weights: λS=0.09\lambda_{S}=0.09 (SIGReg), λT=0.10\lambda_{T}=0.10 (triplet). Optional auxiliary weights (λstr\lambda_{\text{str}} for straightening, γθ,δr\gamma_{\theta},\delta_{r} for the angular planning cost) default to 00; see App. D for the A4 / A5 / A6 sweep.

Appendix D Additional auxiliary-term explorations

While exploring the design space of SD-JEPA we tested several optional auxiliary terms that, in our setup, do not improve the canonical A2 configuration. We document them here for completeness and as a reference for follow-up work. (i) A4 adds the temporal-straightening regulariser ℒstraight=−𝔼⁡[cos⁡(𝒗t,𝒗t+1)]\mathcal{L}_{\text{straight}}=-\mathbb{E}[\cos(\bm{v}_{t},\bm{v}_{t+1})] on the full latent. On Push-T this rung underperforms A2 by roughly 1414 points: applying the straightening cost to the full 𝒛\bm{z} overlaps with SIGReg’s isotropic-Gaussian requirement on 𝒛cont\bm{z}^{\mathrm{cont}}, an instance of the double-counting that Prop. 2 predicts. The same regulariser is the central contribution of Wang et al. (2026), who use it under stop-gradient anti-collapse where the conflict does not arise (Sec. 6). (ii) A5 adds polar (sin⁡θ,cos⁡θ,r)(\sin\theta,\cos\theta,r) conditioning of the predictor’s AdaLN on top of A4 and yields a further ∼2{\sim}2-point drop, suggesting that exposing the angular readout to the predictor at training time over-specialises the content channel without compensating gains. (iii) A6 additionally engages the angular planning cost γθ​(1−cos⁡(θ^−θg))+δr​(r^−rg)2\gamma_{\theta}\,(1-\cos(\hat{\theta}-\theta_{g}))+\delta_{r}\,(\hat{r}-r_{g})^{2} on 𝒛prog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}} at evaluation time. We also tested an auxiliary first-anchor regulariser pulling the genuine first-of-episode frames in each batch toward a fixed reference direction in 𝒛prog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}}, as an attempt to globally calibrate θt\theta_{t} across episodes; this rung returns to the canonical A2 baseline and supports re-engaging the angular planning cost without regression but does not improve over A2 in our setup. We document these explorations to show that the canonical SD-JEPA architecture (A2) does not require any of these extra regularisers, and that adding them tends to interfere with rather than complement the disjoint-supports decomposition.

Additional environments can be further explored such as WorldGym Quevedo et al. (), richer learning approaches directly in the latent Grill et al. (2020), or totally different modalities such as in neuroscience Dong et al. (2024) to observe if we can link such progression metrics to isolate distinct phenomena.

This appendix collects the per-environment latent-geometry figures complementing §5.5. For each environment we ran the latent-compass analysis on the trained checkpoint indicated, on a small set of held-out episodes spanning the dataset’s full episode-id range. Per checkpoint we report (i) the t-SNE projections of 𝒛prog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}} and 𝒛cont\bm{z}^{\mathrm{cont}}, (ii) the trajectory-overlay heatmap of θt\theta_{t} in raw state space, (iii) per-episode signed-Spearman heatmaps against candidate task-progress proxies, and (iv) one frame strip per env exhibiting an interesting non-monotone or multi-phase θ\theta behaviour.

Per-episode signed Spearman against five candidate proxies (Fig. 5) shows that |ρ||\rho| with step_idx is consistently very high (≈0.86\approx 0.86–1.001.00) on all but one episode (ep 8000, the regression case), with block_angle_err and block_goal_dist as close runners-up.

The k=8k=8 checkpoint shows a substantially cleaner S1S^{1} progression manifold: r∈[0.62,0.77]r\in[0.62,0.77] with per-episode std ∈[0.04,0.07]\in[0.04,0.07], angular span 6.16.1 rad (effectively full-circle coverage). The clock advantage seen at k=2k=2 also narrows: mean |ρ||\rho| vs. step_idx drops from 0.910.91 to 0.560.56, with block_angle_err and block_goal_dist reaching |ρ|≈0.56|\rho|\approx 0.56 as well. At k=8k=8 θ\theta is less time-like and more cyclic-phase-like.

E.3 Reacher at kprog=8k_{\mathrm{prog}}{=}8

Mean |ρ||\rho| on Reacher is 0.530.53 for the clock and 0.490.49 for ee_target_dist; on individual episodes the latter beats the clock. joint_speed is essentially uncorrelated with θ\theta (|ρ|≈0.08|\rho|\approx 0.08): θ\theta is not encoding “how fast is the arm moving.” The +3.3+3.3 pp full-z planning lift on Reacher (Tab. 3) is consistent with the angular-cost-on-𝒛prog\bm{z}^{\mathrm{prog}} adding usable information when the latent’s θ\theta is well-coupled to the end-effector-to-goal geometry.

The mean Two-Room |ρ||\rho| is 0.500.50 for the clock and 0.340.34 for agent_target_dist, but the per-episode picture is bimodal: ep 1000 is clock-like (ρ=+0.88\rho=+0.88), ep 7000 is fully task-coupled (ρ=−0.90\rho=-0.90), ep 3000 (Fig. 8) is the cyclic case where Spearman fails. Mutual information or circular correlation would tighten these estimates; we leave that to follow-up work.

E.5 OGBench-Cube at kprog=8k_{\mathrm{prog}}{=}8

OGBench-Cube is the only environment in our suite where a task-physical signal beats the elapsed-time clock in correlation with θt\theta_{t} (mean |ρ||\rho| with block_target_dist is 0.590.59 vs 0.470.47 with step_idx). It is also the environment with the most varied per-episode behaviour: spatial-distance encoding for reaches, gripper-state encoding for picks, and U-cycle encoding for U-shaped paths. The frame strip on episode 500 (Fig. 9) and the 3D t-SNE projections (Fig. 10) capture this variability.

Appendix F Supplementary perturbation analyses

Brief background on head-direction cells.

For readers unfamiliar with the neuroscience analogy invoked in §7: head-direction (HD) cells are neurons in the rodent hippocampal-entorhinal system that encode the animal’s facing direction in the world, independent of location (Taube et al., 1990; Knierim and Hamilton, 2011). Each cell fires preferentially when the head is oriented in a specific allocentric direction; together they form a 1-D circular code where a population peak travels around a circle as the animal turns. Two properties make the parallel with θt\theta_{t} natural: (i) a scalar circular coordinate (a 360∘ heading is collapsed to one moving peak), and (ii) re-mapping under perturbation, when the environment is teleported, rotated, or otherwise restructured, HD-cell populations re-anchor their peak to the new visual cues and then track coherently from there, the same kind of structural re-localisation we observe in θt\theta_{t} after our teleport-and-continue perturbation. We do not claim our latent rediscovered the biological circuit; the parallel is qualitative, two systems converging on a similar geometric solution (a single circular phase coordinate ++ re-mapping under sensory restructuring) for what is broadly the same problem.

The main text headlines the teleport-and-continue perturbation (Figure 3), in which the “moment” (latent surprise spike) and the “meaning” (post-perturbation relocalisation in θ\theta) come apart cleanly. Three complementary perturbation modes confirm and refine that picture. All run on Push-T A2 (canonical, kprog=2k_{\text{prog}}=2, seed 30723072, epoch 10), processed by the same encoder with no test-time fine-tuning.

Splice (Figure 11).

We replace all frames of episode 00 from step 5050 onward with frames from episode 10001000. Unlike the headline teleport-and-continue — which uses an episode-pair chosen to maximise the visual contrast in solving mode, the splice picks an arbitrary substitute scene. Result: a ≈0.17\approx 0.17 rad surprise spike at the boundary (∼8×\sim 8\times baseline mean), followed by sustained elevated noise across steps 5050–7070 as the encoder processes the unfamiliar trajectory. The post-perturbation θt\theta_{t} diverges from the clean baseline but does not pin to a single new sector; instead it traces a new path consistent with the new episode’s progression. This is a weaker but still positive surprise signal, the magnitude depends on how angularly distinguishable the donor episode is from the original.

Single-frame teleport (Figure 12).

We insert a single frame from a structurally different scene at step 5050 of episode 00, then resume episode 00. The angular surprise spikes to ≈0.20\approx 0.20 rad at the substituted frame and returns to baseline within a single step, a textbook illustration of localised surprise with immediate recovery. The model registers the anomaly, reports a sharp θ\theta jump, and resumes normal localisation as soon as the genuine observation stream returns. This mode tests recovery dynamics: when the perturbation is transient, relocalisation is also transient.

Reverse-window perturbation (Figure 13).

We reverse a 10-frame window of episode 00 starting at step 4040. Critically, the set of frames presented to the encoder is unchanged — only the temporal order is altered. Any angular discontinuity in this mode must therefore be a model-dynamics phenomenon, not a scene-novelty artifact. The result: matched spikes of ≈0.11\approx 0.11 rad at the window’s leading boundary (step 4040) and ≈0.13\approx 0.13 rad at the trailing boundary (step 5050), with elevated noise within the reversed window. This rules out the alternative hypothesis that the surprise spikes in the splice and teleport modes are simply registering “a novel scene appeared”; they are registering “the dynamics violated the model’s local expectations”, which is the stronger and more interesting claim.

Animated GIF for talks / online supplementary.

The same teleport-and-continue experiment renders as an animated GIF via analysis/surprise_voe.py --gif --mode teleport_continue. The animation marks the perturbation frame with a red border + “TELEPORT” overlay text and switches the on-screen θt\theta_{t} trace from blue (pre-perturbation) to red (post-perturbation), making the relocalisation visible in real time. The static Figure 3 carries the same information for the paper.

Appendix G Phase-event localisation vs. classical surprise: extended results

This appendix collects the full empirical evidence for the comparison between |Δ​θt||\Delta\theta_{t}| and z-MSE as surprise signals on OGBench-Cube (§5.5, Tab. 4, Fig. 2). The headline finding is that the two metrics measure complementary things: |Δ​θt||\Delta\theta_{t}| is the right tool for semantic-event localisation, z-MSE is the right tool for raw magnitude-anomaly detection, and combining them does not improve detection on either test.

G.1 Phase-alignment summary across all 40 episodes

Per-episode AUROC distribution at ±2\pm 2-step tolerance:

metric median mean IQR
|Δ​θ||\Delta\theta| 0.4720.472 0.4700.470 [0.415,0.544][0.415,0.544]
z-MSE 0.3530.353 0.3580.358 [0.312,0.421][0.312,0.421]

Both AUROC distributions sit below 0.50.5 at the tight ±1\pm 1-step tolerance: z-MSE peaks during the stable-contact phase (when the cube is being translated while gripped) rather than at the transitions themselves, and only ∼11%{\sim}11\% of all steps are positive labels. |Δ​θ||\Delta\theta|’s peaks are consistently closer to transitions even when not exactly aligned, so widening the tolerance window catches more of those near-aligned peaks and pushes |Δ​θ||\Delta\theta| above 0.50.5 before z-MSE follows. The right reading is the gap, not the absolute level.

G.2 Action-corruption AUROC: the magnitude-anomaly negative control

To verify that the two metrics genuinely measure different things, we run a complementary test where the corruption is a magnitude anomaly rather than a semantic event. We replace a contiguous 25%25\% band of each episode’s actions with a random shuffle and ask each metric to localise the corrupted band as a per-step random-segment AUROC.

env corruption z-MSE |Δ​θ||\Delta\theta| combined (rank-sum)
Reacher action shuffle 0.771\mathbf{0.771} 0.6570.657 0.7360.736
Reacher other-episode 0.808\mathbf{0.808} 0.6630.663 0.7630.763
Push-T action shuffle 0.598\mathbf{0.598} 0.4960.496 0.5530.553
Cube action shuffle 0.696\mathbf{0.696} 0.6590.659 0.6940.694

z-MSE wins this test by construction: the action-shuffle injects a magnitude anomaly that a 192192-dimensional MSE detects more sensitively than a 11-dimensional phase scalar; the per-step random-segment label rewards information bandwidth, not semantic alignment. The combined rank-sum score does not beat z-MSE on any cell; the two metrics are not strictly orthogonal but are clearly answering different questions.

G.3 Regime-change segmentation (change-point detection)

A second formulation of the same hypothesis: at semantic phase events, θt\theta_{t} exhibits a regime shift (different mode of evolution before vs. after) while z-MSE just spikes and returns to baseline. We run BinSeg with K=4K=4 requested change points on the 4040 cube episodes and compute precision/recall/F1 against the ground-truth contact transitions with greedy 1-to-1 matching at tolerance ±\pmtol.

metric F1 ±1\pm 1 F1 ±2\pm 2 F1 ±3\pm 3
|d​θ/d​t||d\theta/dt| (observed angular vel.) 0.3940.394 0.6130.613 0.812\mathbf{0.812}
z-MSE 0.481\mathbf{0.481} 0.769\mathbf{0.769} 0.7750.775
|Δ​θ||\Delta\theta| (prediction error) 0.4250.425 0.7250.725 0.7440.744

The regime-change test is a partial vindication: at loose tolerance the observed angular-velocity trace beats both prediction-error metrics, but at tight tolerance z-MSE’s spike-and-return pattern produces sharper change-point boundaries that BinSeg locates more accurately. This is consistent with the AUROC reading: |Δ​θ||\Delta\theta| excels at peak alignment with semantic events, z-MSE excels at sharp magnitude-spike segmentation; both are useful and the choice depends on what the practitioner wants to detect.

Appendix H Cross-machine reproducibility note

Trainings ran on a mix of H100 GPUs and (for Push-T) RTX 5090 GPUs; all evaluations are on H100. Single-seed checkpoints exhibit non-trivial planning-success variance across these microarchitectures even when training data, config, and seed are identical. Concrete observation: a SD-JEPA kprog=4k_{\mathrm{prog}}{=}4 checkpoint trained on an H100 at seed 00 evaluates to 100%100\% on Push-T; the analogous re-train on an RTX 5090 at the same seed evaluates to 94%94\%, a 6-point gap on identical configuration. We attribute this to non-bit-deterministic bf16 matmuls across tensor-core kernels, dataloader shuffling sensitivity to num_workers, and library version pinning differences across the two machines. Multi-seed averaging absorbs the variance: the 3-seed Push-T means at kprog=4k_{\mathrm{prog}}{=}4 and kprog=8k_{\mathrm{prog}}{=}8 (96.096.0 and 97.397.3) sit cleanly within LeWM’s own reported single-environment σ=2.83\sigma=2.83. We therefore treat ≥n=3\geq n=3 multi-seed means as the reportable comparison granularity throughout the paper.
